headline: Highest risk is data leakage: ms-swift handles secrets and files while emqx has broad network egress, creating a plausible exfiltration path; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are lower but present.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared clipboard, MCP, or filesystem bridge is documented, so direct injection is not proven. However, ms-swift reads/writes files and emits stdin/stdout, while emqx exposes an HTTP API and broad network egress, so a manual or scripted content bridge could carry malicious instructions. The pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF the operator pipes emqx output into ms-swift stdin/stdout or shared files, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF either agent is configured to treat file or API content as trusted instructions, attacker-controlled text can steer behavior.
mitigations: Disable any file-to-stdin automation between the agents.
Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Add an explicit instruction/content delimiter in any handoff file.
Review and sanitize any emqx-generated text before ms-swift consumes it.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to all inter-agent handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles secrets and reads/writes files, while emqx has broad network egress and touches IoT data. Even without a documented shared workspace, the pair can leak sensitive material if ms-swift outputs are forwarded through emqx or if emqx relays file contents. The interaction is inferred from documented capabilities, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF ms-swift processes hub_token or sdk-token in files or logs, those values can be exposed to emqx via forwarded outputs.
IF emqx is used to relay or publish ms-swift artifacts, sensitive IoT or configuration data can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in shared files or logs.
Use separate directories with restrictive permissions.
Redact tokens before any handoff to emqx.
Restrict emqx egress destinations to known endpoints.
requires-engineering: add secret-scanning on inter-agent outputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can execute shell commands, install packages, spawn subprocesses, and write the filesystem; emqx has broad network egress and HTTP API access. Their write and network capabilities overlap on mutable resources, so concurrent use can conflict even though emqx is not documented as writing files. Lack of stated locking or isolation increases uncertainty, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory or service, writes can race or overwrite each other.
IF ms-swift installs packages while emqx is running in the same environment, dependency or runtime state can diverge.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Avoid concurrent package installation during emqx operation.
Run one agent at a time for shared resources.
Lock any shared config files before edits.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level resource locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can produce model outputs, logs, and evaluation artifacts, and emqx can move data over HTTP with broad egress. If emqx consumes ms-swift output as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream actions or publications. No verification or provenance controls are documented, so the safer reading is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF emqx forwards ms-swift-generated text without validation, hallucinations or malformed outputs can propagate.
IF ms-swift evaluation outputs are treated as ground truth by emqx, downstream decisions may be wrong.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before forwarding outputs.
Require schema validation on ms-swift artifacts.
Mark all inter-agent data as untrusted by default.
Log source provenance for each forwarded item.
requires-engineering: implement automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift handles hub_token and sdk-token and touches datasets, checkpoints, and logs, while emqx touches IoT data and has broad network egress. If regulated or region-bound data flows from ms-swift into emqx, residency or retention mismatches are plausible. No explicit compliance controls are documented for either agent, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF EU PII, PHI, or other regulated data is processed by ms-swift and then sent through emqx, residency or retention obligations may be violated.
IF emqx logs or republishes ms-swift artifacts, retention policies can diverge.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared flows.
Configure minimal retention on logs.
Separate regional deployments by data class.
Redact tokens and identifiers before transfer.
requires-engineering: document and enforce a data-processing agreement and residency policy.
